Safety

Drones aren't dangerous. Careless pilots are.

▶  Present the slides

Drones, batteries and soldering irons are a lot of fun, and some of it is hot, fast or full of energy. This guide collects every safety page from the HOBIzone Quick Guides in one place. When a new guide adds a safety slide, it shows up here too.

Drones aren't dangerous. Careless pilots are.

Almost all accidents come from the person holding the sticks: rushing, not checking, not paying attention. Only a few come from the drone or the radio link. That's good news: it's in your hands.

Props off on the bench

On the bench or in the pits a drone can start by itself: a bump on the switch, a wrong setting, a stuck radio. Spinning props cut. So: props off, then battery. Fix it, set it up and test the motors without props. Props go on only at the flying area, just before you fly.

Battery out before you touch it

A drone can spin up again even when it looks off. Before you pick it up, carry it or touch a prop: disarm, wait for the props to stop, then unplug the battery. Hear a beep or see a light? It's live.

Burns

A soldering iron tip is 350–400 °C: hotter than a pizza oven. If you get burnt: cool it under running water for 20 minutes, take rings and watches off, use burn spray or gel from the first-aid kit after cooling and cover it loosely with cling film, and always tell your trainer. Know where the first-aid kit and burn spray are before you switch the iron on. A big burn (bigger than your palm, on the face or hands, or with big blisters): call 112.

Safe at the soldering bench

Glasses on: solder and flux can spit. A fan or fresh air, so you don't breathe the smoke. The iron goes back in its stand every time you let go; hold the handle, never the metal. Wash your hands after soldering and keep food and drinks off the bench. Switch the iron off when you're done and let it cool before packing it away. And no LiPo plugged in while you solder.

Look after your batteries

A LiPo battery holds a lot of energy. Never charge without someone watching, charge in a LiPo bag on stone or metal, never charge or fly a swollen or damaged battery, and unplug when it's full. Old or puffy batteries go in the battery collection box, never in the bin.

Why a LiPo burns

A LiPo doesn't burn like paper. It starts with damage: a crash, a puncture, overcharging or a short. One cell gets hot inside, the heat breaks down the next layer, which makes even more heat: a chain reaction called thermal runaway. First it puffs and hisses and gives off white, poisonous smoke, then it can burst into jets of flame. Because the battery makes its own heat, you can't just "switch it off" or smother it like a candle. And a battery that looked finished can flare up again hours later.

Battery fire: what to do

You: get away, shout "Battery fire!" so an adult comes, and never touch it: it's over 500 °C and the smoke is poisonous. Adults, only if it's safe: unplug the charger at the wall and move away anything that can burn. A fire blanket or LiPo bag can keep the fire from spreading, but it won't put it out. Cool the battery with lots of water. A LiPo is a lithium-ion battery, and fire services say water is the right choice: it cools the cells and stops the fire spreading from cell to cell. Powder and CO₂ extinguishers only knock the flames down, and the pack flares up again. (The "never use water" rule you sometimes read is for lithium-metal batteries, like some non-rechargeable cells. A LiPo has no lithium metal.) When it has stopped hissing and spitting, move it outside with a shovel or tongs into a metal bucket of water. Sand is a safe surface to stand it on, but it doesn't cool the pack, so don't bury a hot pack in sand. A burnt pack can flare up hours later: leave it in the water outside for at least 24 hours (the Rescue Board says 2 to 3 days), then take it to a jäätmejaam. Don't breathe the smoke: it contains poisonous gases, including hydrogen fluoride. If the fire is big or spreading: get out, close the door and call 112. Everyone should know where the water bucket, the fire blanket and the exit are.

Flying together

Book your channel on the reservation screen before you plug in, and wait your turn if someone is on it. Video power is never higher than 25 mW. Say it out loud: "Plugging in!", "Taking off!", "Landing!", "Crash!". Stay in the pilot area and never fly over or towards anyone.

The rules outside the club

Outside our training hall drones follow EU rules, run in Estonia by Transpordiamet. Register as an operator if your drone weighs 250 g or more or has a camera, and put your operator ID on the drone. Pass the free online A1/A3 test, required from 250 g, and a good idea for everyone. Stay below 120 m and away from people, roads and buildings. Check no-fly zones at utm.eans.ee. Flying FPV? A spotter must stand next to you and watch the drone, even with a drone under 250 g. (Under 250 g, FPV with a spotter is allowed in A1; Transpordiamet confirmed this in 2026.) Rules change. Check transpordiamet.ee.

Under 16? The coach is the pilot

You have to be 16 to take the A1/A3 test and get certified. Until then you may fly bigger drones only under the direct supervision of a pilot who is certified. Only toys and home-built drones under 250 g have no age limit. That's why our outdoor training and official races always happen in a designated area, under a coach's supervision: the coach is the responsible pilot. Planning to fly on your own and you don't have a certificate? Don't fly alone. Take a licensed adult with you, and they are the responsible pilot. Flying FPV? You still need a spotter.

Before, during, after

Check the drone, props and battery before you fly; keep it in sight, watch the battery and land in time while you fly; disarm, unplug, check and clean up after.

Drones aren't dangerous. Careless pilots are.
